Items.Authors: Jules Fowler, Rebecca Jensen-Clem, Sylvain Cetre, Maaike A. M. van Kooten, Maïssa Salama, Antonin Bouchez, Avinash Surendran, Charlotte Guthery, Eduardo Marin, Mahawa Cissé, Max Service, Charlotte Z. Bond, Emiel Por, Nour Skaf, Will Gauvin
Items.Title: Ground control to major time-lag: on-sky results of data-driven predictive wavefront control at Keck Observatory
Items.Abstract: Directly imaging and characterizing exoplanets requires extreme adaptive optics (XAO), to achieve exquisite wavefront correction over a small field of view. Predictive wavefront control (PWFC) mitigates temporal errors (often a leading term in these XAO systems) by predicting where the wavefront will be by the time the system correction is applied. In particular, empirical orthogonal functions (EOF) learn correlations in a wavefront using wavefront sensor history. We present on-sky results of a new implementation of EOF built directly into the Keck-II real time controller (RTC). This work revitalizes previous PWFC work at Keck, by showing improved performance over an integral controller during on-sky observing. Finally, we discuss optimization strategies for EOF on sky. This work not only improves current observing for the Keck community, but also acts as a pathfinder for predictive control methods with extremely large telescopes.

Items.Authors: Mark Mueller, Andrew Szentgyorgyi, Sagi Ben-Ami, Isaac Anderson, Daniel Baldwin, Daniel Durusky, Ofir Hershko, Colby Jurgenson, Kenneth McCracken, Heeyoung Oh, Jae Sok Oh, Cem Onyuksel, William Podgorski, Chan Park, Matthew Smith, Yahel Sofer-Rimalt, Abigail Unger, Joseph Zajac
Items.Title: Hardware fabrication update for the GMT-consortium large earth finder (G-CLEF)
Items.Abstract: The GMT-Consortium Large Earth Finder (G-CLEF) is a fiber-fed, optical echelle spectrograph that will be a first light instrument for the Giant Magellan Telescope (GMT). G-CLEF is a general-purpose echelle spectrograph with precision radial velocity (PRV) capability. We will design and build an interim installation configuration for G-CLEF at Magellan’s 6.5m Clay telescope. This paper provides an update on construction of the instrument. It discusses the fabrication and integration of several completed subsystems including the optical bench, vacuum chamber, major optical subassemblies, the Clay front end, electrical systems, and fixturing.

Items.Authors: Amelia Calderhead, Anna MacIver, David Isherwood, Andy Born, James Stevenson
Items.Title: HARMONI at ELT: developing a modular review process using TRIZ
Items.Abstract: The HARMONI team at UKATC have been pioneering the use of TRIZ by managing monthly TRIZ workshops to tackle significant project problems that arise. This TRIZ case study investigates how design changes of HARMONI can be reviewed effectively and efficiently. It draws on how the review process of Ground Based Astronomy projects can be improved to add quality to the successful creation of an instrument while reducing strain on designers and reviewer’s time.   To address resource-intensive and document-driven review processes, the case study utilised TRIZ techniques including; thinking in time & scale technique: the 40 inventive principles to tackle design contradiction: function analysis and size, time, cost analysis.  The solution developed considered a modular, continuous review process focusing on specific subsystems or technical topics as they mature while encouraging a live review culture, where stakeholders and expert reviewers are engaged continuously through informal check-ins.

Items.Authors: P. Bañares-Palacios, M. A. Cagigas, A. A. Luján González, B. García-Lorenzo, A. Alonso, A. de Lorenzo-Cáceres
Items.Title: HARMONI at ELT: integral field spectrograph pre-optics (IPO) design after rescope process
Items.Abstract: HARMONI is the first light, adaptive optics assisted, near-IR integral field spectrograph for the ELT. It covers a spectral range from 750nm to 2450nm with resolving powers from 3000 to 7000 and spatial sampling of 25mas and 6mas. It can operate in two adaptive optics modes - SCAO (including a high contrast capability) and MCAO. The project is resuming its final design phase after a rescope design phase in 2025.     The instrument faced budgetary constraints that led to a reduction in the number of available scales in the IPO subsystem. An overview of the process and final design is presented, where 4x4mas, 10x10mas, 20x20mas and 60x30mas scales (in addition to the pupil imaging scale for alignment, which was preserved) were substituted by 6x6mas and 25x25mas scales, compromising technical requirements and scientific needs.

Items.Authors: Rafael Melgar Hernandez, Yolanda Martin, Elvio Hernández Suárez, Alejandro Antonio Luján González, Alberto Hernández González, Horacio Rodriguez Delgado, Felix Gracia Témich, Miguel Angel Cágigas García, Ángel Alonso, Adriana de Lorenzo Cáceres, Begoña García Lorenzo
Items.Title: HARMONI at ELT: laboratory tests for optimization and validation of the scale changer turret mechanism
Items.Abstract: HARMONI is the first light, adaptive optics assisted, near-IR integral field spectrograph for the ELT. It covers a spectral range from 800nm to 2450nm with resolving powers from 3000 to 7000 and spatial sampling of 25mas and 6mas. It can operate in two adaptive optics modes - SCAO (including a high contrast capability) and MCAO. The project is resuming its final design phase after a rescope design phase in 2025.    This paper reports on the comprehensive testing campaign of the HARMONI IFS Pre-Optic’s (IPO) Scale Changer Turret (SCT) prototype. The primary aim of these tests was to validate the proposed mechanical solution and confirm the overall system performance. We present a detailed analysis of the system and the laboratory setup.

Items.Authors: Eduard R. Muslimov, Matthias Tecza, Edgar Castillo-Domínguez, James Kariuki, Liam Boland, Miriam Cisneros Gonzalez, Kieran McCall, Sophie Paszynska
Items.Title: HARMONI at ELT: optical design of the spectrograph sub-system
Items.Abstract: HARMONI is the adaptive optics assisted, near-IR integral field spectrograph for the Extremely Large Telescope (ELT). The University of Oxford is in charge of the design and development of the four identical spectrographs that disperse the light and form scientific images. During the instrument rescope phase, we have developed a new spectrograph optical design. It uses a two-mirror unobscured freeform collimator, a set of six volume-phase holographic grisms as the disperser, and a two-mirror unobscured freeform camera. This design is up to 350 mm shorter than the previous version. The number of optical elements' positioning parameters is reduced by more than two times. The expected as-built minimum transmission is 62.3%, while the scattered light level is decreased.

Items.Authors: Vladislavs Plesanovs, Paolo Soffitta, Hemanth Manikantan, Daniel Saueraland, Klaus Desch, Jochen Kaminski, Carlo Lefevre, Ettore Del Monte
Items.Title: Heavy ion irradiation of GridPix gas detector: a step forward for its use in space
Items.Abstract: The GridPix technology is a candidate to be used as a polarimeter on the potential successor  of IXPE, the EXPO or Enhanced X-ray Polarimetry Observatory. Dedicated set of runs was performed at Bonn Isochronous Cyclotron at HISKP, University of Bonn, to test heavy ion influence in MeV energy range. In a gasseous detector these particles induce overwhelming amount of charge that can saturate the electronics readout or induce sparks and rapidly age the detector. GridPix was subjected to two test beams at a low rate, proton beam at 14MeV and 100MeV 14N5++ ions. The GridPix detector contains the readout ASIC, Timepix, with 256 × 256 pixel grid with a pitch of 55 μm and covered with a protection layer plus gas. The Al grid stands on the SU8 pillars above pixels forming the amplification stage enabling primary electron detection. We describes the setup and results of these tests. The observed impact of irradiation is shown for both types of beam.

Items.Authors: Robert Conwell, Stephen S. Eikenberry, Peter Delfyett, Anish Roshi, Shahebul Hasan, Jiabao Li, Jordan Richey, David Smith, Thuy Nguyen, Amith Debnath, Liam Gallagher
Items.Title: Heliocomb: a laser frequency comb heterodyne spectrometer for R=20,000,000,000 solar observations
Items.Abstract: We demonstrate a near-infrared heterodyne instrument which achieves a signal-to-noise ratio sufficient for Very Long Baseline Interferometry (VLBI). VLBI in the near-infrared, achieved by means of heterodyne systems, has the potential to enable ground-based diffraction-limited resolution of millimeter-sized objects in low Earth orbit. Our instrumental design employs an electro-optically modulated laser frequency comb (LFC) as a single-frequency local oscillator with tunability enabled by a calibrated linear stage. Our design is conducive to an instrument with the long-term stability of a LFC, a tunable local oscillator, and scalability for broad instantaneous bandwidth. To demonstrate the efficacy of our instrument, we perform heterodyne spectroscopy on the Sun to measure the Solar Gravitational Redshift, improve upon the current best measurement, and demonstrate year-timescale instrumental stability. This is an essential first step towards near-infrared VLBI.

Items.Authors: Manon Lizzana, Fabien Malbet, Hugo Rousset, Sébastien Soler, Fabrice Pancher
Items.Title: High precision differential astrometry
Items.Abstract: Differential astrometry measures the position and motion of celestial objects relative to nearby stars. Missions like Hipparcos and Gaia reached microarcsecond precision, and future missions such as NASA’s HWO and ESA’s Theia aim for sub-microarcsecond accuracy, enabling studies of Galactic dark matter and the detection of Earth-mass exoplanets.    This work presents key elements of a high-precision astrometric instrument and the simulations of the calibrations required to reach this accuracy. We characterize the 46Mpx Gigapyx CMOS detector from Pyxalis, showing its strong potential for future astrometric focal planes. Sub-microarcsecond precision corresponds to 10⁻⁵ (HWO) or 10⁻⁶ (Theia) pixels on the detector. It requires micro-pixel mapping of gigapixel-scale detectors and optical distortion calibration thanks to high-order polynomial models. We introduce the IPAG (Grenoble) testbed enabling these measurements.

Items.Authors: Chris Hamner, Sebastien Vievard, Akinyele Gilbert, Aidan Walk, Elsa Huby, Sylvestre Lacour, Guillerme Martin, Teruyuki Hirano, Motohide Tamura, Takayuki Kotani, Olivier Guyon
Items.Title: High resolution Echelle Spectrometer integrating 19 channel photonic lantern
Items.Abstract: In exoplanet science, high-resolution spectroscopy enables the identification of companions with narrow emission lines and the isolation of giant exoplanets, as well as facilitating the measurements of orbital velocities, masses, and molecular signatures. We aim to develop a high-throughput spectro-imaging solution that simultaneously provides the benefits of single mode fiber (SMF)-spectroscopy, and accesses spatial and spectral information below the telescope diffraction limit. We propose a design for a single mode Echelle spectrometer that accepts simultaneous input from a photonic lantern (PL) having 19 single mode fiber (SMF) outputs. In addition to the 19 SMF input channels, the spectrometer is designed to separate each channel into linear polarization states, resulting in 46 spectral measurements (38 stellar channels and 8 calibration channels). The design and fabrication status for the spectrometer will be presented.

Items.Authors: Bhushan Joshi, Nicolas Erasmus, Willem Smit, A. N. Ramaprakash, Kathryn Rosie, Hitesh Gajjar
Items.Title: High-cadence, AI-assisted sCMOS camera for time-domain astronomy
Items.Abstract: We propose a small, AI-assisted sCMOS camera designed for quick transient detection. The system combines an NVIDIA Jetson Orin module, scalable FPGA control circuits, and a low-noise sCMOS sensor to carry out CNN-based transient classification and real-time image correction at the telescope. This local operation reduces latency and data transfer. Designed with adaptability in mind, the architecture can be extended to support upcoming astronomical applications such as multi-detector arrays or CubeSat-based instruments.

Items.Authors: Benjamin Calvin, Jessica Castellanos, Michael Fitzgerald
Items.Title: High-contrast aperture masking interferometry: using a vortex coronagraph for detecting companions within the diffraction limit
Items.Abstract: The search for the direct discovery of exoplanets has motivated high-contrast imaging surveys using coronagraphs with narrow inner working angles. Traditional imaging methods are limited by the size of the on-axis PSF and are not sensitive to companions at close separations. Meanwhile, non-redundant masking (NRM) techniques are used with single-aperture telescopes to resolve astrophysical features within the diffraction limit, but NRM interferometry faces sensitivity issues at high contrasts. In these proceedings, we investigate simulations utilizing high contrast coronagraphy in conjunction with NRM interferometry. The vortex coronagraph delivers an improvement in the relative throughput of a close-separation companion, which improves the sensitivity of the interferometric observables. This preliminary investigation introduces the conceptual architecture for combining these techniques and explores the potential discovery space for high contrast targets within the diffraction limit.

Items.Authors: Quan Zhang
Items.Title: High-precision image stabilization control strategy for large space astronomical telescope
Items.Abstract: The precision image stabilization subsystem of the large space astronomical telescope usually incorporates a fast steering mirror(FSM) and several fine guide sensors (FGS). The Fine Guide Sensor, serving as the detection module of the precision stabilization system, is located at the edge of the main field of view and shares the primary optical system with the main focal plane. The FGS first carries out the high-frame-rate star target extraction and positioning, then calculates these extracted star points to output both relative attitude information (line-of-sight deviation of the space telescope) and absolute attitude information (three-axis orientation of the telescope). The piezoelectric-driven large-aperture fast steering mirror, serving as the actuator in the precision image stabilization system, is responsible for compensating line-of-sight deviations and fine pointing adjustment.

Items.Authors: Yuyao Liu, Yonghui Hou, Teng Xu, Jiangfang Hua, Xuhao Wu, Wei Wei, Chao Liu, Yue Sun, Hang Zhang
Items.Title: High-stability vacuum delay line for optical interferometry: mechanical deformation analysis and optical performance evaluation
Items.Abstract: We present a study on the mechanical and optical performance of a high-stability vacuum delay line designed for optical interferometry. The system operates under a moderate vacuum level of 10⁻³ atm and aims to ensure structural rigidity and stable optical propagation. Finite element and optical modeling were used to evaluate the deformation behavior and resulting wavefront quality. The results indicate that the delay line maintains sufficient stability for interferometric applications, demonstrating its suitability for future extensions toward longer delay strokes and enhanced measurement precision.

Items.Authors: Giovanni Della Casa, Francesco Ceraudo, Ettore Del Monte, Giuseppe Dilillo, Marco Feroci, Edoardo Giancarli, Alessio Nuti, Riccardo Campana, Mauro Fiorini, Giovanni Lombardi, Massimo Rapisarda, Ajay Sharma, Giuseppe Bertuccio, Filippo Mele, Yinhe Zhu, Marco Grassi, Piero Malcovati, Jacopo Giani, Marco Tambussi, Matias Antonelli, Alexander Rachevski, Irina Rashevskaya, Gianluigi Zampa, Nicola Zampa, Evgeny Demenev, Giancarlo Pepponi, Francesco Ficorella, Nicola Zorzi, Alessandro Gemelli, Alina Samusenko
Items.Title: High-throughput spectral-timing with large-area SDDs
Items.Abstract: The Large Area Detector (LAD) is an instrument concept based on an array of collimated large-area linear Silicon Drift Detectors (SDDs). Its design was specifically developed to perform optimal spectral resolution and timing studies in the 2-30 keV band. A prototype of LAD with lower number of anodes was coupled with a novel CMOS analog front-end Application-Specific Integrated Circuit (AFE ASIC), named NOVA, to demonstrate the performances of the combined instruments, in view of future mission proposals. In this work, we will present the spectral resolution results obtained for the integrated detector system (NOVA ASIC and SDD prototype) as a function of operational parameters.

Items.Authors: M. Lebreton, Q. Guer, P. Gellie, J. C. Roche, D. Darson
Items.Title: HIRIS, the low-noise and high-dynamic hyperspectral imager project
Items.Abstract: Short-wave infrared wavelengths open our vision beyond the visible spectrum, bringing useful contrast to situations and applications where visible or thermal imaging cameras are ineffective. This presentation introduces HIRIS, a low-noise and high-dynamic hyperspectral imager based on the existing SIRIS SWIR camera. The low-signal sensitivity is limited by the blackbody radiation emitted by all objects at ambient temperature (300 K), seen by the sensor within the field of view (FOV) of the camera. In multispectral imaging, low-noise efficiency is altered when using an uncooled filter wheel. Adding a cooled SWIR filter inside the original camera vacuum chamber makes possible to avoid the parasitic signal. Tunable filter selection regarding low-noise considerations, modeling, and integration are introduced. Early results, obtained with a first uncooled prototype are discussed.

Items.Authors: Jean-Baptiste Ruffio, Charles Kilpatrick, Bryson Cale, Ben Sappey, Ashley Baker, Max Brodheim, Tim Brandt, Aidan Gibbs, James D. Neill, Samuel Halverson, Quinn Konopacky, Chase Beichman, Graham Bruce Berriman, Rob Bertz, Ava DeLaGarza, Jocelyn Ferrara, Luke Finnerty, Michael Fitzgerald, Rose Gibson, Katelyn Horstman, Nem Jovanovic, Marc Kassis, Stephanie Leifer, Andrea Lin, Jeff Mader, Dimitri Mawet, Jason Wang
Items.Title: HISPEC data reduction pipeline II: H4RG detector calibrations and up-the-ramp data processing
Items.Abstract: HISPEC is a new high-resolution spectrograph (R>100k) currently being built for the W.M. Keck Observatory with simultaneous 0.98-2.5 μm wavelength range coverage. HISPEC is equipped with two H4RG-10 detectors which were spares of the Roman Space Telescope. We will describe the first stage of the HISPEC data reduction pipeline (stage 0) which aims at processing the up-the-ramp data to generate fully calibrated electron rate maps. The pipeline needs to be both extremely accurate to enable precise radial velocity measurements (<30 cm/s) and computationally efficient to continuously process the multiple terra-bytes of data generated per day with HISPEC.

Items.Authors: Davide Ricci, Simone Doniselli, Matteo Aliverti, Luigi Lessio, Davide Greggio, Lorenzo Cabona, Silvano Tosi, Filippo Zerbi, Sandro Zappatore
Items.Title: How to turn a small observatory into a multi-instrument facility for photometry, long slit, and échelle spectroscopy
Items.Abstract: Observatories of class up to 1m are commonly provided with COTS cameras for imaging/photometry. This is especially true for didactic, outreach, and private telescopes, although they are also successfully used for scientific purposes.  Spectroscopy is generally relegated to larger, institutional facilities and their corresponding professional instruments. However, semi-professional solutions exist. How to integrate them in small observatories?  We present the first light of Cerberus, a three-headed instrument for the 80cm OARPAF telescope in Northern Italy: a new Nashmyth interface flange allows connecting not only the existing SBIG CCD camera, but also a LHIRESIII long slit and a FLECHAS échelle spectrograph. Moreover, the photometry mode is upgraded with a tip-tilt lens to correct for tracking and vibrations at a 10Hz rate.  The three instruments are alternatively selected through a linear stage provided with mirrors, and are remotely operated by a custom web-based graphical interface.

Items.Authors: Chao Tang, Arwa Dabbech, Adrian Jackson, Yves Wiaux
Items.Title: HyperAIRI: A Physics-informed Plug-and-play Algorithm for Hyperspectral Image Formation in Radio Interferometry
Items.Abstract: Next-generation radio interferometers will produce extremely large, wideband observations that require precise and scalable imaging methods. We present HyperAIRI, a new hyperspectral imaging algorithm designed to meet this demand by combining optimization theory and deep learning, with an overall algorithmic convergence guarantee. HyperAIRI alternates a data-fidelity step with a regularization step via learned hyperspectral deep-neural-network denoisers. Each spectral channel is processed in parallel using denoisers matched to its dynamic range, informed by its neighboring channels and a physically motivated power-law spectral model. A shelf of networks spanning typical dynamic ranges provides further flexibility. Tests on simulated and real observations show that HyperAIRI delivers state-of-the-art imaging precision compared with existing optimization-based and CLEAN-based approaches, while preserving the efficiency of the monochromatic AIRI framework.

Items.Authors: Luca Girolimetto, Emanuele Simioni, Claudio Pernechele, Giovanni Costa, Paolo Martini, Matteo Massironi, Javier Eduardo Suarez-Valencia, Diego Scaccabarozzi, Chiara Martina, Kirill Potemkin, Luigi Lessio, Adriano Tullo, Cristina Re, Leonardo Amoruso, Carmela Agnese De Donno, Marco Mucci Beltrami, Alessandro Varriale, Raffaele Pepe
Items.Title: Hyper-hemispherical structure from motion for lunar cave exploration
Items.Abstract: The paper presents "HH-SfM" (Hyper-Hemispherical Structure from Motion) a global structure-from-motion algorithm developed for the ESA Daedalus mission to explore and map Moon caves using a robot with a hyper-hemispherical lens system. The goal is to reconstruct the robot’s trajectory and environment during its descent into a lava tube. The system’s rig consists of four cameras, allowing each cave point to be seen by at least three cameras. The algorithm optimizes the rig's position and triangulated points using a global bundle adjustment, incorporating odometry for scale correction. The resulting geometry enables photogrammetric reconstruction for geological analysis and exploration of Moon channels, with potential applications on Earth.

Items.Authors: Sebastiaan van der Tol
Items.Title: IDG‑CAL: estimating continuous corrections for wide‑field imaging
Items.Abstract: Image Domain Gridding (IDG) is an efficient method to evaluate A-projection, a method for  correcting for direction dependent effects (DDEs) in radio astronomical imaging.  The corrections i.e. the A-terms need to be estimated from the observed data   through calibration. IDG-CAL is a calibration algorithm that employs   the IDG algorithm in an iterative fashion to estimate A-terms directly.  Initial results for low order A-terms are promising, however for  deeper images higher order A-terms are needed.  Here two improvements to IDG-CAL are proposed to 1) reduce the computational cost  of A-terms described by more parameters and 2) optimize the set of basis  functions describing the A-terms based on a stochastic model of the gain variations  and the model image.

Items.Authors: Christian Eredia, Vincenzo Cianniello, Enrico Cascone
Items.Title: Implementation of extended reality in the development process of astronomical instrumentation
Items.Abstract: An eXtended Reality (XR) laboratory has been created in the Astronomical Observatory of Capodimonte, in Naples, in the scope of the National Recovery and Resilience Plan project "STILES - Strengthening the Italian leadership in ELT and SKA".  The laboratory is supporting the design process of the new generation of astronomical instrumentation. An upgrade of the XR equipment has already taken place, with the aim of building multi-user sessions, which prove to be extremely useful both for design reviews and especially for training and testing maintance operations.  The laboratory has been transferred to its ultimate location, in the Naples Concurrent Design Facility, where the XR technologies have been paired with the tools already installed in the facility, starting also to support the first concurrent design sessions.   This paper describes both the upgrades made on the hardware side, and the activities that are being carried out by exploiting the acquired techonologies.

Items.Authors: Paul Rabe, Carel van Gend, Nicolas Erasmus, Stephen Potter, Ruby George
Items.Title: Implementing telemetry as part of the SAAO Intelligent Observatory initiative
Items.Abstract: This work describes the development of a unified telemetry system for the SAAO Intelligent Observatory initiative. The system collects real-time operational data, including environmental metrics, subsystem states, logs, and audio streams, and ingests them into a central FastAPI-based service with PostgreSQL storage. PyTorch-based autoencoders perform real-time audio anomaly detection, and operators access dashboards for system status, spectrograms, and alerts. A standard JSON telemetry format ensures consistent data submission while requiring only minor client-side adaptations for each subsystem. Lightweight acquisition nodes, including Raspberry Pi devices, capture and forward local telemetry. All software components are open-source, free from licensing restrictions, and supported by active development communities. The system provides improved situational awareness, increased automation, and supports predictive maintenance across SAAO facilities.

Items.Authors: Michael R. Vissers, Logan Howe, Andrea Giachero, Pietro Campana, Corwin Shiu, Maya Erickson, Jordan Wheeler, Johannes Hubmayr, Joel Ullom
Items.Title: Improved inverted microstrip kinetic inductance traveling wave amplifiers for detector array readout
Items.Abstract: Kinetic inductance traveling wave (KIT) parametric amplifiers based on NbTiN have demonstrated gain >20dB across several gigahertz of usable bandwidth, added noise of less than a photon more than the quantum limit. and sufficient dynamic range to read out large numbers of superconducting resonators. However, difficulties in integration into readout chains suitable for large arrays of devices have limited their impact. Here, we discuss significant progress on improving the design, microwave launch, microwave ground, as well as replacing the previously needed bulky, lossy, commercial components with superconducting on-chip replacements. These improvements result in high performance devices with beyond octave bandwidth that are far more compact and show reduced gain ripple and insertion loss than previous iterations. We will also discuss preliminary results on scaling the amplification bandwidth to higher (>20GHz) and lower (1GHz) frequency bands.

Items.Authors: Masaki Numazawa, Manabu Ishida, Yuichiro Ezoe, Naoya Sera, Ryo Kishikawa, Atsuto Matsumura, Mai Takeo, Asca Miyamoto, Tsubasa Uchino, Kumi Ishikawa, Yoshitomo Maeda, Daiki Ishi, Kohei Morishita, Kazuo Nakajima
Items.Title: Improvement of imaging performance of silicon foil x-ray optics using hot plastic deformation process
Items.Abstract: We have been developing silicon foil X-ray optics using hot plastic deformation for future astronomical observations. A 0.3-mm-thick silicon wafer was formed into a precise conical shape with a curvature radius of ~100 mm. Owing to the favorable physical properties of silicon, these mirrors offer reduced weight and improved angular resolution compared to conventional aluminum foil optics. Process optimization achieved an angular resolution of 27.4 arcseconds along the best generatrix—a twofold improvement over previous results—evaluated at the ISAS/JAXA 30-m X-ray beamline. This paper presents fabrication improvements and enhanced X-ray imaging performance of the silicon foil optics.

Items.Authors: Gianluca Marotta, Matteo Di Carlo, Stefano Di Frischia, Elisabetta Giani
Items.Title: Improving observability and reliability in SKA control software through TANGO-controls open telemetry and CSP.LMC test analytics
Items.Abstract: In the Square Kilometre Array (SKA) project, early detection of rare and hard-to-reproduce anomalies is essential to ensure system reliability. SKA software components, built on TANGO-Controls and deployed as Kubernetes-orchestrated containers, can exhibit unpredictable or non-deterministic behaviour that must be closely monitored. To improve insight into such failures, the Central Signal Processor Local Monitoring and Control (CSP.LMC) subsystem has begun collecting detailed test-failure statistics and benchmarking data. With the introduction of OpenTelemetry support in TANGO-Controls, new observability capabilities have become available. This work explores how combining Tango OpenTelemetry instrumentation with CSP.LMC’s test-result collection framework can enhance anomaly detection, strengthen performance benchmarking, and improve software quality across the SKA ecosystem.

Items.Authors: Timothy Butterley, David Barr, John Connolly, Thomas Davies, Sofia Dimoudi, Kathryn Hartley, Linn Htat Lu, Luke Johnson, Timothy Morris, Emily Ronson, Dirk Schmidt, Jurgen Schmoll
Items.Title: Increasing the sensitivity of a solar Shack-Hartmann turbulence profiler to high-altitude turbulence
Items.Abstract: Ground based solar telescopes require multi conjugate adaptive optics (MCAO) to achieve the best possible resolution, which in turn requires detailed knowledge of the atmospheric turbulence profile. The profile can be measured using a solar version of the slope detection and ranging (SLODAR) technique, using a wide field Shack-Hartmann wavefront sensor (WFS) that measures wavefront slopes by tracking image motion. As well as overall motion, subaperture images also contain distortions due to differential tip/tilt variations. Usually these are regarded as a noise source but we propose to measure them in order to derive extra information about high altitude turbulence and hence improve the profile resolution. We present Shades, a method of measuring WFS image distortions, and demonstrate how turbulence profiles can be derived from these measurements. We apply this method to experimental data from the Nēnē solar SLODAR turbulence profiling instrument on the DKIST telescope.

Items.Authors: Ryan J. Oelkers, Luke M. Schmidt, Moises Castillo, Erika Cook, Richard Camuccio, Eric Gonzalez, Carlos Francile, D. L. DePoy, Mario Díaz, Horacio Dominguez, Diego G. Lambas, Lucas M. Macri, Jennifer Marshall, Federico Podesta, Ernesto M. Schnieter, Marcelo Segura
Items.Title: Infrastructure and instrument upgrades in support of the Transient Optical Robotic Observatory of the South (TOROS) at the Felix Aguilar Observatory
Items.Abstract: The Transient Optical Robotic Observatory of the South (TOROS) is a newly commissioned ground-based observatory deployed to the Felix Aguilar Observatory in San Juan, Argentina. TOROS was designed to provide optical follow-up of potential gravitational wave sources, and a planned upgrade during the August of 2026 will enable TOROS to obtain rapid response color observations for transient events and variable stars discovered by the NSF-DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory’s Legacy Survey of Space and Time (Rubin-LSST). Here we report on the planned infrastructure and instrument upgrades to modernize the Felix Aguilar Observatory including our plans for the full robotization of the facility, on-site automatic data reduction, and integration into several alert streams. The observatory has already achieved first light, and we expect full operations to start in the fall of 2026 to coincide with the first year of Rubin-LSST operations.

Items.Authors: Ross Cheriton, Emma Rautio-Roe, Glen Herriot, Alexis Hill, Brent Carlson, Siegfried Janz, Thushara Gunaratne, Zoran Ljusic, John Weber, Martin Vachon, Shurui Wang, Nicaulas Sabourin, Jianhao Zhang, Dan-Xia Xu, Pavel Cheben, Jens H. Schmid
Items.Title: Integrated silicon photonics for long baseline optical aperture synthesis
Items.Abstract: Optical aperture synthesis is the most promising route towards achieving the very high spatial resolution required to resolve features on exoplanets themselves. However, the required baselines are on the order of tens of kilometers, which makes phasing each receiver extremely challenging in the optical regime. Integrated photonics can provide a scalable and stable platform for optical beamforming that can compensate for atmospheric turbulence. We outline our experimental progress towards a photonic aperture synthesis proof-of-concept instrument which uses a photonic integrated circuit to achieve coherent phasing and combination of light from multiple receivers.

Items.Authors: Nyasha J. Suliali, James M. Ivory, Konstantin D. Stefanov, David Hall, Manish R. Patel
Items.Title: Integrated UV and optical scientific CMOS sensor characterisation with in-built quality control
Items.Abstract: Electro-optical characterisation of a scientific CMOS sensor has been demonstrated. Characterisation of the sensor in the 200 to 400 nm wavelength region, on an integrated bench setup with a single control panel has been demonstrated. This paper outlines the construction, calibration and integration of the supervisory, control, data acquisition, processing and reporting functions on a single platform for seamless sensor characterisation. Critical characterisation aspects such as in-built sub-system quality control, total test duration and measurements of selected parameters such as the dark current and photo response from 20 °C down to -25 °C are presented.

Items.Authors: Ismam Abu, Fulvio Gianotti, Andrea Bulgarelli, Pietro Bruno, Luca Castaldini, Isaias Huerta, Vito Conforti, Mattia Corpora, Alessandro Costa, Ambra Di Piano, Federico Fiordoliva, Valentina Fioretti, Stefano Gallozzi, Andrea Giuliani, Alessandro Grillo, Federico Incardona, Marcello Lodi, Saverio Lombardi, Fabrizio Lucarelli, Andrea Mandica, Emilio Mastriani, Kevin Munari, Nicolò Parmiggiani, Giovanni Pareschi, Valerio Pastore, Federico Russo, Pierluca Sangiorgi, Salvatore Scuderi, Alessandro Tacchini, Gino Tosti, Sebastiano Spinello
Items.Title: Integration of the ICT Kubernetes Cluster with the SCADA system for the ASTRI Mini-Array project
Items.Abstract: The ASTRI Mini-Array is an INAF-led project deploying nine dual-mirror Cherenkov telescopes for very-high-energy gamma-ray astronomy. Seven telescopes are installed, and two are already acquiring Cherenkov data during commissioning. A dedicated ICT infrastructure supports installation and operations, integrating network services, a virtualization platform, a computing cluster, distributed storage, and auxiliary systems.  Kubernetes is adopted as the computing platform to provide scalability, resilience, and efficient orchestration of SCADA subsystems, including Kafka, Cassandra, MongoDB, and InfluxDB, together with ASTRI-specific monitoring and data-quality services. CI/CD pipelines with integrated GitLab runners enable reproducible and traceable software releases.  This contribution presents the Kubernetes integration with operational services, and key challenges such as containerizing ACS and enabling communication between virtualized and containerized components.

Items.Authors: Tianzhu Hu, Enpeng Zhang, Jian Li, Jialin Tian
Items.Title: Intelligent Temperature and Flow Control Methods for Optical Telescope Domes
Items.Abstract: Even at excellent astronomical sites, dome seeing remains a key factor limiting the image quality of optical telescopes. Effective temperature and airflow control inside the dome can reduce dome-induced turbulence, but existing strategies still rely largely on empirical rules and are difficult to apply to large-aperture telescopes with many control devices. The LAMOST dome temperature and flow control team is therefore developing intelligent dome environmental control methods, including a dome seeing monitoring system, a CFD-assisted control method based on dome temperature-distribution measurements, and a reinforcement-learning-based adaptive control method. Preliminary tests on LAMOST show that these approaches can improve spectral image quality, demonstrating their potential for reducing dome seeing and enhancing telescope performance.

Items.Authors: Xiaodong Ren, Jón E. Guðmundsson
Items.Title: Investigating polarization effects in the Simons Observatory Large Aperture Telescope using a novel physical optics code
Items.Abstract: The Simons Observatory Large Aperture Telescope (SO LAT) is designed to deliver high-fidelity measurements of cosmic microwave background (CMB) polarization, and therefore requires precise control and modeling of instrumental polarization across a wide field of view. We present an efficient Physical Optics (PO) framework that combines a two-step PO method for the large crossed-Dragone reflector with a hybrid-PO analysis for the cold refractive optical tubes. This approach captures the frequency-dependent transmission and polarization properties of lenses with sub-wavelength structures, such as the silicon lenses used on SO LAT. Using the resulting beams and Mueller-matrix patterns across the focal plane, we quantify key polarization systematics, including temperature-to-polarization leakage and Q/U mixing arising from optical non-idealities.

Items.Authors: Joel Payne, Jonathan Steiner, Jason N. Worden, Ben McCarney, Joseph Rounsaville, Max Davis, Michael Dayawon, Steve Baca, Danny Baldwin, Justin Ballard, James Chong, Michael Dahler, Matthew Dolloff, Hamza Elwir, Robert Harrington, Grant Hill, John S. Hudek, Edward Janke, Rick Johnston, Eric LeVine, Chris Martins, Dennis McBride, Ellie O'Brien, Daniel Orr, Dennis Patterson, Derek Park, Paul Richards, Erin Roberts, Adan Rodrigues, Jacques Sebag, Lauren Simmons, Zach Tadio, Jerez Tehero, John Valliant, Adam Vandenberg, Tod Von Boeckmann, Ed Wetherell, Truman Wold
Items.Title: Investigation and recovery from failed wire ropes at the Keck II Telescope top shutter
Items.Abstract: On July 4, 2025, a significant structural failure of the Keck II top shutter occurred. One of eight wire rope cables supporting the 90,000 lbm shutter failed. Each cable is 5/8” steel and rated for 46,000 lbf working load. The failure was a significant structural problem and presented challenges to diagnose and repair. Operations resumed in August based upon improved system tuning, only for a second failure of two ropes – both controlled by a common drive – to occur on January 22, 2026. Initially, the failures were thought to be separate failure modes. However, closer inspection of data suggested the failures shared more in common than originally realized. The paper presents the investigation, recovery, and a proximate root cause of the drive misbehavior which resulting in the discrepant motion of the drivetrains and eventually wire rope failures. Go forward information and planning is presented on three mitigations: added fault detection, rope tension sensors, and motion encoders.

Items.Authors: Ritika Singh, Christian Pommranz, Michael Freyberg, Emanuele Perinati, Christoph Tenzer, Andrea Santangelo
Items.Title: Investigation of XMM-Newton mirror shell misalignment using ray-tracing
Items.Abstract: Stray light in X-ray telescopes such as XMM-Newton and eROSITA is a well-recognized source of systematic issue, arising primarily from singly reflected photons from either the hyperbolic or parabolic sections of the Wolter-I mirror. Because these instruments employ tightly nested mirror assemblies, isolating a sole contribution to the effective area loss from individual elements using ray-tracing requires a tool capable of accurately simulating such a complex optical design. In this work, we use MARXS (Multi Architecture Raytrace Xray mission Simulator), a Python compatible version of NASA’s MARX (Model of AXAF Response to X-ray) software developed for the Chandra X-ray Observatory. We adapt MARXS to build a detailed simulation of the XMM-Newton mirror module, that will be used to investigate the impact of shell misalignments on the effective area of the instrument.

Items.Authors: Aleksandar Shulevski, Maaijke Mevuis, Pietro Zucca, Alan Wood, Gareth Dorrian
Items.Title: Ionospheric monitoring with LOFAR
Items.Abstract: One key aspect of improving the observational efficiency of the upgraded LOw Frequency ARray (LOFAR) telescope is monitoring the observing conditions, especially at the lowest observing frequencies, to ascertain which science programs can get time on sky. Space weather related ionospheric activity and solar bursts especially at solar maximum can severely limit useful observing windows.    We aim to monitor the ionosphere continuously during operations and construct a metric based (among other inputs) on the ionospheric scintillation index (S4) as well as monitoring solar activity using the observing setup and analysis pipelines developed as part of the Incremental Development Of LOFAR for Space weather (IDOLS) project.    I will present the initial monitoring results obtained during LOFAR commissioning. LOFAR station data reduction and the corresponding metrics will be discussed, as well the plans for their integration into the telescope monitoring and scheduling system (TMSS).

Items.Authors: Armin Silber
Items.Title: Keeping solar energy switched on during nighttime operation. The way forward to a sustainable and green observatory
Items.Abstract: The widespread discussion about renewable energy for Observatories is driven by the commitment to increase the efficiency of energy use hence to save on operational budgets and to reduce the carbon footprint. One of the motivation blockers to invest in sustainable technologies is an existing working infrastructure. In this contribution we will demonstrate on the example of the La Silla Observatory, that the investment is paying off in a reasonable time-frame, when guided by a profound analysis to identify synergies between different energy-consumers. The transformation of a traditional astronomical facility into a sustainable Observatory might inspire the global astronomical community to consider eco-friendly approaches highlighting the benefits of sustainability in reducing operational costs and minimizing the ecological footprint.

Items.Authors: Bin Ma
Items.Title: Laboratory and On-sky Testing of Infrared Camera Candidates for a 40 cm Telescope at Dome A, Antarctica
Items.Abstract: Dome A, Antarctica is recognized as a leading ground-based site for infrared astronomy due to its extremely cold, dry and stable atmosphere. Following the initial deployment of a 15cm Antarctic InfraRed Binocular Telescope (AIRBT) with 640×512 InGaAs cameras in 2023, we are developing a second-generation system with a 40 cm telescope. Two infrared camera options are under evaluation: a 1280×1024 InGaAs camera for a larger field of view, and a 640×512 HgCdTe camera for sensitivity at longer wavelengths. We will perform laboratory tests to measure the fundamental detector properties of both cameras. Then each camera will be integrated with the 40cm telescope for on-sky testing in China. The final camera selection will be based on these technical assessments, aligned with specific scientific objectives for the Dome A.

Items.Authors: Laura Mascetti, Nausicaa Delmotte, Vincenzo Forchì, Stefano Zampieri, Ashley Barnes, Alberto Micol, Diego Rodriguez Mancini, Martino Romaniello, Tomas Tax
Items.Title: Lessons from ESO Phase 3: confronting the challenges of a decade-old system
Items.Abstract: The ESO Phase3 system, the dedicated channel for submitting homogeneous, science-ready data products to the ESO Archive, has become a critical pillar and an invaluable resource for the scientific community. However, its 2016 architecture is now challenged by hardware and software obsolescence, by the steadily growing data volumes from next-generation surveys and increasing demands to support novel data formats.   This contribution details the shortcomings and the necessity of transforming the Phase3 system into a flexible, scalable, and future-proof platform. We illustrate the need for an implementation plan centred on modernising the core infrastructure, enhancing the user experience, and introducing key new capabilities. Even well-established platforms must evolve to meet growing scientific and technical demands, while acknowledging the practical challenges and uncertainties of implementing such changes in real time.

Items.Authors: Pascal Jaufmann, Raphael Seyfang, Jörg-Uwe Pott, Oliver Sawodny
Items.Title: LGS-based vibration control: evaluating closed-loop performance with end-to-end simulations
Items.Abstract: Diffraction-limited imaging in large telescopes requires mitigation of both atmospheric and structural disturbances in the optical system. Therefore, all disturbance acting on the adaptive optics (AO) system must be estimated and compensated for in real-time. We present and compare different methods for the estimation and control of high-frequency vibrations using already available wavefront data from laser guide stars. This includes an integrator combined with a Kalman filter as well as linear quadratic Gaussian control. The designs are validated within a realistic end-to-end AO simulation fed by telemetry data from the Very Large Telescope.

Items.Authors: Anne-Laure Cheffot, Davide Orsucci
Items.Title: Long-baseline infrared interferometry using quantum communication networks in Europe
Items.Abstract: In recent years, several publications have suggested that technologies and infrastructure developed for quantum communication could be leveraged to enable long-baseline interferometry. In this article, we provide an overview of the proposed technologies, their current capabilities, and the infrastructure being deployed across Europe. We examine how long-baseline infrared interferometry can benefit from these systems and which adaptations would be necessary to meet its specific requirements.

Items.Authors: Kirtan P. Dixit, Danielle N. Gurgew, Panini S. Singam, Jessica A. Gaskin, Stephen D. Bongiorno, Nicholas E. Thomas, David D. Smith
Items.Title: Machine learning-based inverse design of X-ray multilayers for high energy astrophysics missions
Items.Abstract: An end-to-end machine-learning framework is under development to design depth-graded multilayer (DGM) coatings for full-shell grazing-incidence optics from science requirements. The pipeline takes as input a target effective-area–versus–energy curve, telescope geometry, grazing-angle range and number of mirror shells, and works backwards to find a coating design for each shell so that the combined optic reproduces the requested response. A fast physics-based reflectivity calculator is coupled to machine-learning models that propose DGM recipes, followed by an optimization stage that adjusts shell reflectivities to better match the target effective area. Initial studies focus on hard X-ray telescope designs, and the framework is structured to extend to other energy bands and optical layouts. The goal is a practical tool that shortens multilayer optimization time and clarifies trade-offs between science performance, coating complexity and fabrication limits for future space telescopes.

Items.Authors: B. Borguet, C. Bastin, V. Moreau, B. Carlomagno, M. Quesnel, G. Orban de Xivry, J. van der Maas, L. Violleau
Items.Title: MADOCS: a high-speed adaptive optics control system for optical communications
Items.Abstract: We present MADOCS, a high-speed adaptive optics (AO) system derived from the SALTO demonstrator and engineered for free-space optical communication on a 1-m-class telescope. Designed to operate outside traditional observatory conditions, the system must accommodate rapid satellite slews and therefore achieve higher control bandwidths than typical AO used in astronomy. MADOCS employs two independent control loops: a 4 kHz tip–tilt loop using a fast-steering mirror for pointing stabilization, and a 2.5 kHz deformable-mirror loop for higher-order correction. Laboratory evaluations under controlled turbulence conditions demonstrate stable, low-latency closed-loop operation. By the time of the conference, we expect to present on-sky results showing the practical transfer of astronomical AO techniques to the more demanding temporal and pointing-stability requirements of optical communication.

Items.Authors: Helen M. McGregor, Jon Moller, Dylan Simpfendorfer, Jahanzaib Zahoor, Zhemin Cai, Jon Lawrence, Celestina Lacombe, Jessica Zheng, Chris Coote, Lew Waller, Nirmala Kunwar, Tony Farrell, Tayyaba Zafar, Michael Goodwin, Vitor Neves Hartmann
Items.Title: MANIFEST for GMT, conceptual design for the fibre positioner
Items.Abstract: MANIFEST is a fibre-positioning system for the Giant Magellan Telescope (GMT) that will feed light from hundreds of deployable probes into high- and medium-resolution spectrographs, including G-CLEF and GMACS, across 350–1000 nm and future infrared instruments. Initially covering the corrected 14′ field-of-view, MANIFEST will later expand to the full 20′ field-of-view. It offers single fibres, multiple integral-field-units, and image-slicing for enhanced resolution and wavelength coverage. Key capabilities include high multiplexing, simultaneous multi-instrument observations, and adaptability for future instruments. Using a pick-and-place robotic system, MANIFEST will significantly boost GMT’s survey efficiency and scientific productivity. In this paper we present the conceptual design overview for MANIFEST.

Items.Authors: Jonathan Moller, Zhemin Cai, Dylan Simpfendorfer, Jahanzaib Jahoor, Helen McGregor, Jon Lawrence, Celestina Lacombe
Items.Title: MANIFEST for GMT, structural design during CoDR phase
Items.Abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive finite element analysis (FEA) of the updated MANIFEST mechanical architecture for the Giant Magellan Telescope (GMT). Following the transition from Starbug robots to a pick-and-place fiber positioning system, the design now incorporates a curved metal field plate, magnetic fiber buttons, four robotic arms and mechanisms to move the field plate between operating positions. These structural changes introduce new mechanical challenges requiring validation across gravity, thermal, and dynamic loading conditions. Detailed FEA models were developed to evaluate deformation, stress, and modal behaviour for the field plate, corrector field lens group, and the integrated system. Simulations include gravity-induced displacement under multiple orientations, thermal expansion across operational and survival ranges, and dynamic response under varying preload conditions.

Items.Authors: Jonathan Moller, Zhemin Cai, Christopher Coote, Jessica Zheng, Dylan Simpfendorfer, Jahanzaib Zahoor, Celestina Saavedra Lacombe, Michael Goodwin, Jon Lawrence, Helen McGregor
Items.Title: MANIFEST for GMT: conceptual opto-mechanical design
Items.Abstract: This paper describes the current conceptual design of the opto-mechanical components, mechanisms and general instrument architecture that enable MANIFEST to perform effectively under the Giant Magellan Telescope’s operational conditions. The instrument features several hundred probes connected to optical fibres precisely positioned over a curved field plate, which requires to change position to allow four pick-and-place robots to reach the probes and deploy them in different field configurations. The science observations are performed once the field plate is positioned at the focal plane where a large Field Lens corrects and focuses the light into the micro lens array and prism fitted inside each probe.

Items.Authors: M. Becerril-Tapia, M. Baghoria, P. S. Barry, T. L. R. Brien, S. Doyle, C. J. Dunscombe, H. Gordon-Moys, A. Manning, S. Rowe, C. S. Woodhead
Items.Title: Mapping large CMB-KID arrays through LED scanner
Items.Abstract: Kinetic Inductance Detectors (KIDs) are widely used in the development of large-format cameras in the millimetre/far-infrared range. Due to minor non-uniformities inherent in their manufacturing, there are uncontrolled variations in the detectors' resonance frequencies, leading to overlaps or interactions between two or more resonators. Modifying the resonance frequencies of one or more resonators by controlled changes in their capacitance can correct these collisions. This work presents the development and performance of a cryogenic LED scanner for mapping detectors. We show the latest results from mapping large KID arrays of Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) detectors (>400), characterising their resonator properties, including quality factors and dispersion of resonance frequencies. Having the resonator collisions located, we lithographically trim their capacitors, decoupling the resonances and improving array yield.

Items.Authors: Zain Azam, Aditya Khandelwal, Ryan Dungee, Ting S. Li, Sarik Jeram, Shaojie Chen
Items.Title: Measuring the linear gain performance for the OrcaQuest CMOS imaging sensor
Items.Abstract: The OrcaQuest CMOS sensor by Hamamatsu Photonics has been found to exhibit a non-linear gain curve at low exposure times. This effect is characterized through the various exposure tests and data reduction pipelines detailed in this report, and a more accurate gain characterization curve is provided. Such data can be used to provide more consistent measures of pixel gain, linearity, and high framerate images.

Items.Authors: Lawrence Bissell, Éamonn J. Harvey, Stephen Todd, Alastair Macleod, Valentina Oyarzun, Daniel Dicken, Katherine Morris, Philip Parr-Burman, Alistair Glasse, Felix Bettonvil, Bernhard Brandl
Items.Title: METIS for ELT: optical alignment and testing of the IFU of the LM-band spectrograph
Items.Abstract: The METIS LMS (LM-band Spectrograph) is a high-resolution (R>100,000) mid-infrared integral field spectrograph for the ESO ELT. The instrument provides the capability to measure instantaneous spectra across a 0.577 x 0.897 arcsecond field-of-view with a spatial sampling of 8.2-9.1 mas using an image slicing IFU. This paper presents the optical testing and alignment performed for the IFU sub-system including: the detailed characterisation of the image slicing mirror array and an overview of the optical alignment strategy to be employed during the AIT process,.

Items.Authors: Dennis Dolkens, Peter Bizenberger, Harald Baumeister, Bernhard Brandl, M. Concepcion Cardenas Vazquez, Eduardo Chamorro, Silvia Scheithauer, Takashi Sukegawa
Items.Title: METIS: grism spectroscopy in the mid-IR
Items.Abstract: METIS, the Mid-infrared ELT Imager and Spectrograph for the ELT offers mid-infrared grism spectroscopy in the atmospheric L, M & N bands. We describe the optical design, the cryogenic mounting, manufacturing and verification results of these three grisms. They have been developed and produced in close collaboration with CANON, Japan.   Particularly, wavefront and transmission measurements at component level are presented. Setup of test stands and results of verification are outlined and presented. Key parameter is the anti-reflection coating in order to achieve a high throughput with Germanium substrates.
